references.text: The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, is first mentioned when Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh with the message to let the people go to offer sacrifices.
Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh with the same message: 'Let my people go, so that they may hold a feast for me in the wilderness.'
The same command from the Lord to Pharaoh: 'Let my people go, so that they may serve me in the wilderness.'
The Lord again commands Moses to go to Pharaoh with the message: 'Let my people go, so that they may serve me.'
Repeated command to Pharaoh: 'Let my people go, so that they may serve me.'
Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh once more with the Lord's word to let the people go.
Pharaoh's servants ask how long Moses will be a snare to them and urge letting the Israelites go.
The Lord asks how long the people will despise him, a similar rhetorical question about persistent disobedience.
The wording 'humble oneself' (ענה) is used regarding Pharaoh who refused to humble himself before the Lord.
An appeal to humble oneself under God's mighty hand, in contrast to Pharaoh's pride and refusal.
The original formulation of the demand for 'service' that forms the foundation for all subsequent demands.
The contrast between Pharaoh's offer to 'sacrifice' and God's demand to 'serve' reveals Pharaoh's mistaken understanding of freedom.
Repetition of the 'serve' formulation confirms God's consistent goal throughout the course of the conflict.
Pharaoh's temporary humiliation (Ex 9:27) contrasts with God's ongoing demand to 'humble oneself' in Ex 10:3.
Direct narrative connection: God's demand for humility (Ex 10:3) is met by Pharaoh's admission (Ex 10:16).
Pharaoh's attempt to restrict service in Egypt (Ex 8:21) contrasts with God's demand for freedom to serve (Ex 10:3).
